name: Cantonese
confidence_why: Chao 1947 states outright that stress never affects the identity of a Cantonese word, Lee 1993 and Wong, Chan and Beckman 2005 independently deny any contrast between stressed and unstressed syllables, and the only hint of word stress, an iambic pattern Bauer, Cheung, Cheung and Ng 2004 suspected from the duration of two personal names, is one they say they did not investigate.
catalog_citation: Chao, Yuen Ren. 1947. Cantonese Primer. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press (Harvard-Yenching Institute). Part One, Introduction, ch. II 'Pronunciation and Romanization', section 13 'Stress'.
catalog_locator: p. 36 (archive.org item yuen-ren-chao-cantonese-primer-1947), section 13 'Stress', between section 12 (pinn'iam / changed tone) and section 14 'Junctures' read
catalog_quote: 13. Stress. — Stress is not a constituting element of words in Cantonese as it is in Mandarin or English. Of course all syllables in Cantonese are not pronounced with the same degree of force or heard with the same degree of loudness. But the variation depends upon the sounds concerned and upon the relative prominence of words in the sentence determined by stylistic factors. The identity of words in Cantonese is never affected by stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Yue Chinese/Cantonese is not in the catalog. Of the five stress-title items, none is a first-hand word-stress description: Williams 1856 'Tonic Dictionary' (downloaded from archive.org) is about tones and only separates tone from 'accent'; Lee et al. 2024 (abstract, paywalled) is child bilingual intonation; Bauer, Cheung, Cheung & Ng 2004 (downloaded from the SEALang SALA archive and scanned, 21 pp.) is about sentence-level focus-stress (duration is the main cue) with a tentative side remark that bisyllabic words 'may carry inherent word-stress on the second syllable' (pp. 35-36, 39); Wong, Chan & Beckman 2005 (paywalled OUP; abstract via Crossref) states the 'absence of contrast between stressed and reduced (neutral tone) syllables' and is the one item worth acquiring in full (priority high); the Glottolog 'Jun 2005' entry is a duplicate of that chapter credited to the compilers. The best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title remains Chao 1947 Cantonese Primer p. 36 (already held by the project): 'Stress is not a constituting element of words in Cantonese.. The identity of words in Cantonese is never affected by stress' -> no-word-stress.org, Crossref, Unpaywall and the SALA archive index.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Cantonese is a tone language (six to nine tones plus the derived 'changed tone' pinn'iam) in which stress plays no role at the word level: there is no lexically or positionally fixed word stress, and no word is distinguished by stress. Perceived loudness differences between syllables follow from the segments themselves and from sentence-level prominence set by stylistic (focus/emphasis) factors.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Chao contrasts Cantonese explicitly with Mandarin (where neutral tone / stress is word-constituting) and English.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level explicitly denied; prominence is sentence-level and stylistic. Later instrumental work (Lee et al. 2002, saved) finds word-final rime lengthening with slightly higher F0/intensity on non-final syllables but does not call this stress; FSI 1970 speaks only of sentence stress. Chao describes the Canton (Guangzhou) standard as taught at Harvard in 1942-47.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Chao 1947 describes standard Cantonese of Canton (Guangzhou) as taught at Harvard 1942-47; Zee 1991, Lee et al. 2002, Wong 2004 and Man 2002 describe Hong Kong Cantonese. Both are the Guangzhou-Hong Kong standard variety of Yue (yuec1235 is the language-level code; Glottolog has no separate accepted glottocode for standard Cantonese distinct from Yue). The statement does not cover other Yue lects (Taishan/Siyi, Nanning Baihua, Tengxian) listed in Glottolog's yuec1235 bibliography.

English has contrastive stress; Cantonese, on the other hand, has stress, but does not use it contrastively. [p. 41] ... Within native Cantonese words, there is a perceptual connection between stress and high tone (Hashimoto 1972: 101-102). According to Hashimoto, syllables that have the Upper Ascending [35] tone, the Upper Even [53] or [55] tone, and the high Upper Entering [5] tone are stressed more heavily than syllables bearing other tones. For example, in "egg yolk" [tA:n 33 wO:ng 35], [wO:ng] is stressed more strongly than [tA:n] [p. 42]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with Chao 1947 ('Stress is not a constituting element of words in Cantonese.. identity of words is never affected by stress'): Lee likewise denies contrastive word stress. She adds (citing Hashimoto 1972 and Kiu 1977) that the perceived prominence is a function of tone, not of position, and that Cantonese loanword phonology maps English stress onto the high tone. The dissertation has no stress or prosody section; Introduction pp. 1-2 discusses tone versus pitch accent only in general typological terms.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Cantonese is a tone language with a phonetic stress difference that is never lexically contrastive; following Hashimoto 1972, syllables carrying the high tones (35, 53/55, high entering 5) are perceived as more heavily stressed than syllables with other tones, and in English loanwords the English stressed syllable is rendered with the high level tone (55/53), an unstressed word-final syllable with the changed tone 35, other unstressed syllables with 33. No positional word-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; the passage is about exceptional tone-vowel pairings in loanwords and onomatopoeia
new_statements.identity_note: Lee 1993 describes 'standard Cantonese' (Guangzhou/Hong Kong standard variety) and, in the quoted passage, English loanwords in Cantonese; her informant for the acoustic study spoke with a Tengxian accent (p. 71). Wong 2002 is on Hong Kong Cantonese. Wong 2006 (not opened) is explicitly Hong Kong Cantonese. All are the same Glottolog variety yuec1235.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's no-word-stress coding from Chao 1947 ('Stress is not a constituting element of words in Cantonese'): Wong finds no phonological stress markers and no neutral tone, and rejects reading fusion as evidence of word stress. It adds the detail that trochaic/iambic word-stress analyses have been proposed (Chan 1985; Lee 2003) but are judged unwarranted; no placement rule is given, so nothing contradicts the record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hong Kong Cantonese is treated as a tone language without a word-stress system: it has no neutral-tone (reduced) syllables, the author finds no reliable phonological markers comparable to Mandarin 'stress' or to a dominant sandhi syllable, and she argues that syllable-fusion facts do not warrant positing an underlying trochaic (Chan 1985) or iambic (Lee 2003) word-stress pattern; the bisyllabic 'foot' she invokes is a pure grouping unit (C_ToBI), not a prominence unit, and in fusion neither syllable is 'dominant' (tone is the last thing to go).
new_statements.exceptions: She notes earlier proposals of trochaic (Chan 1985) or predominantly iambic (Lee 2003) word stress for Cantonese and leaves the question open pending perception studies ('the idea is interesting for further exploration'); no perception study of Cantonese stress existed as of 2006.
new_statements.identity_note: Wong 2006 describes Hong Kong Cantonese connected speech (speakers from Hong Kong); the catalog record (Chao 1947) describes standard Cantonese of Canton; the three HKU theses concern Hong Kong Cantonese.

tone_statements.quote: There are six lexical tones (T) and three allotones in Hong Kong Cantonese (Bauer & Benedict, 1997). Each syllable (usually corresponding to a morpheme) carries a tone. The six lexical tones are: T1 (high-level [55]), T2 (high-rising [25]), T3 (mid-level [33]), T4 (low-falling [21]), T5 (low-rising [23]), and T6 (low-level [22]). ... The three allotones are traditionally called the “entering tones” in Chinese phonology. They only appear in syllables ending with unreleased stops [-p, -t, -k]: T7 (high-stopped [5]), T8 (mid-stopped [3]), and T9 (low-stopped [2]).

tone_statements.quote: Cantonese is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken in Hong Kong, Macau, and Guangzhou (Eberhard et al., 2020). [...] These lexical tones are distinguished by pitch height, contour, and magnitude of change (Fok, 1974; Gandour, 1981; Khouw & Ciocca, 2007). Among these six tones, there are three level tones (T1, T3, T6), two rising tones (T2, T5), and one falling tone (T4). The level tones mainly differ in pitch height: T1 has the highest pitch, followed by T3, followed by T6, which has the lowest pitch. The rising tones are characterized by a rising contour, with T2 ending at a higher pitch than T5. Finally, the falling tone, T4, is produced with a falling contour and typically contains considerable glottalization (Yu & Lam, 2014).

readall_conflicts: No contradiction. The catalog's statement of record (Chao 1947: stress is not a constituting element of words; 41-42: Cantonese 'has stress, but does not use it contrastively'; heavier stress is perceived on high-tone syllables, after Hashimoto 1972) both deny lexically contrastive word stress in a tone language. The only difference is terminological: Chao frames the non-contrastive force differences as segment- and sentence-dependent, Lee/Hashimoto tie them to tone height. Neither gives a positional rule, so the tentative iambic word-stress remark from Bauer et al. 2004 (earlier reading, two test words, 'not investigated') remains unsupported by any of the six works here. Four of the six works could not be opened (Wong 2006, Kwan 2005, Wong S.Y. 2005, Lam 2004); Wong 2002 was opened and is silent.

sources.quote: 13. Stress. — Stress is not a constituting element of words in Cantonese as it is in Mandarin or English. Of course all syllables in Cantonese are not pronounced with the same degree of force or heard with the same degree of loudness. But the variation depends upon the sounds concerned and upon the relative prominence of words in the sentence determined by stylistic factors. The identity of words in Cantonese is never affected by stress.

sources.quote: Cantonese utilizes a boundary tone, which is realized as a salient final-syllable F0 rise that overrides lexical tones (Chen, 2020; Ge & Li, 2019). When questions end with T23 (low rising) which is contingent with boundary tone, T23 under boundary tone accelerates its F0 rise to approximate T25 (high rising). [...] In Cantonese, yes-no questions diverged from statements at the final syllable, while intonation questions overlapped with statements until the final syllable's midpoint before sharply rising to mimic T25.

sources.quote: Compared to Mandarin Chinese, modern Cantonese has a more complex tonal system (cf. Figure 1.1 of Ou, 2012), featuring six lexical tones (T1 to T6) and three allotones (with similar pitch values to T1, T3, and T6 but differing in duration, namely T7, T8, and T9) [...]. Several similar pairs of Cantonese tones, such as T2-T5 (two rising tones), T3-T6 (two level tones), and T4-T6 (a low-falling tone and a low-level tone), share the same or similar tonal contour, differing only in subtle pitch distinctions. [...] at the group level, the younger generation in Macau has completed the merging of the T2-T5 tones, with no significant differences in mean, slope, and curvature between the two tones (ps > 0.05). The T3-T6 tones have not yet completed the merging, showing a significant difference in mean (p = 0.01). Additionally, the T4-T6 tones have not completed the merging either, with significant differences in all three features (ps < 0.05).

sources.quote: Cantonese is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken in Hong Kong, Macau, and Guangzhou (Eberhard et al., 2020). It has six lexical tones that occur on open syllables with optional nasal codas (Bauer & Benedict, 1997; Matthews & Yip, 2013). [...] These lexical tones are distinguished by pitch height, contour, and magnitude of change (Fok, 1974; Gandour, 1981; Khouw & Ciocca, 2007). Among these six tones, there are three level tones (T1, T3, T6), two rising tones (T2, T5), and one falling tone (T4). The level tones mainly differ in pitch height: T1 has the highest pitch, followed by T3, followed by T6, which has the lowest pitch. The rising tones are characterized by a rising contour, with T2 ending at a higher pitch than T5. Finally, the falling tone, T4, is produced with a falling contour and typically contains considerable glottalization (Yu & Lam, 2014).

sources.quote: The use of lexical tone (T) is a salient phonological characteristic of Cantonese. Each syllable (usually corresponding to a morpheme) carries a tone. Cantonese has a complex tone system. There are six distinct lexical tones based on pitch contrast alone: T1 [55] high–level, T2 [25] high–rising, T3 [33] mid–level, T4 [21] low–falling, T5 [23] low–rising, and T6 [22] low–level (Fok-Chan, 1974; Bauer & Benedict, 1997). [...] There are three allotones which are traditionally called the ‘entering tones’ in Chinese phonology. They only appear in syllables ending with unreleased stops [-p, -t, -k]: T7 [5] high–stopped, T8 [3] mid–stopped, and T9 [2] low–stopped. [...] Although Cantonese is a tonal language, whereas English has lexical stress with multiple acoustic cues, it has been repeatedly demonstrated that pitch is an important, if not the most important, cue in English stress perception.
sources.locator: pp. 1358 (tone inventory), 1368 (tonal language vs; English lexical stress)
sources.note: Longitudinal auditory analysis of Cantonese tone production by five simultaneous Cantonese-English bilingual children at 2;0 and 2;6 versus monolinguals, finding early delay and a high-low template resembling English trochaic stress.

sources.quote: Cantonese encodes pitch in tones for lexical meanings. As is illustrated in Figure 1, there are six lexical tones in Cantonese (Chao, 1947; Bauer & Benedict, 1997). The six tones are labeled according to Bauer and Benedict (1997) as follows: T1, a High Level (55) tone; T2, a High Rising (25) tone; T3, a Mid-Level (33) tone; T4, a Low Falling (21) tone; T5, a Low Rising (23) tone; T6, a Low Level (22). The six tones are contrastive in meaning. For example, /si 55/ 'silk', /si 25/ 'history', /si 33/ 'to try', /si 21/ 'time, /si 23/ 'city', /si 22/ 'matter'. There are also three checked tones: T7, a High level (5); a Mid-Level T8, (3); T9, a Low Level (2). The three checked tones are shorter in duration, but they do not differ from the three corresponding level tones in pitch patterns.

A minimal contrast set for these six Cantonese tones is illustrated by the words /si55/ `poem', /si35/ `history', /si33/ `attempt', /si21/ `time', /si23/ `city', /si22/ `trained person'.

sources.quote: A word as to the tones may be useful here. The necessity for acquiring the exact values of the tones cannot be urged too strongly. Cantonese pronounced with wrong tones is absolutely meaningless, and differs in this respect from Mandarin where it appears that it is possible to make oneself understood without troubling much about the tones. (p. ix) ... IV.—TONES. Average musical value / Suggested name. 1st Tone: upper falling (with variant uppermost level). 2nd Tone: upper rising. 3rd Tone: upper level. 4th Tone: lower falling. 5th Tone: lower rising. 6th Tone: lower level. (p. xiv) ... the so-called jap ('entering') tones are not really special tones at all, their musical values being identical with those of the tones known as soeng-ping and ha-hoey respectively. The differences between words falling under the classes soeng-ping and soeng-jap, or ha-hoey and ha-jap are differences of articulation, not of musical tone. (p. xvii) ... Vowels not followed by a consonant in the same word are usually long, though they may become short if the word is unimportant. In words ending in p t or k the vowels are extremely short. (p. xvi)

sources.quote: Tone and juncture phenomena of special interest for prosodic typology include: the rather strict monosyllabicity of Cantonese word forms; the absence of contrast between 'stressed' and reduced ('neutral tone') syllables; and the extremely dense syntagmatic tonal specification, including non-segmental boundary tones. All three characteristics set Cantonese apart from Mandarin Chinese.

sources.note: Abstract only: the C-ToBI conventions chapter states that Cantonese has no contrast between 'stressed' and reduced (neutral-tone) syllables, i.e. no word-level stress contrast of the Mandarin type; word forms are strictly monosyllabic and no reliable intermediate prosodic grouping between syllable and intonational phrase is found. Unpaywall reports no OA copy; OUP page serves navigation only to direct download and could not be reached by automated download. Full text would give the most explicit modern phonological statement.
